definition: A collection of distinct objects, called its elements, where order and repetition do not matter. Sets are the basic building block for functions, relations, graphs and types in discrete maths.
example: {1, 2, 3}, {3, 1, 2} and {1, 1, 2, 3} are all the same set, with three elements.

definition: x ∈ A means "x is one of the things in the set A". The symbol ∈ is a stylised Greek epsilon and is read "is an element of" or "is in".
x ∉ A means "x is not one of the elements of the set A". It is the negation of x ∈ A.
A ⊆ B ("A is a subset of B") means every element of A is also an element of B. A set is always a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set.
A ⊂ B means A is a subset of B but not equal to it: B has at least one element that A lacks. Some books use ⊂ to mean ⊆ instead, so check the convention.
The unique set with no elements, written ∅ or {}. Its size is 0. It is a subset of every set, but it is an element of a set only if that set lists it explicitly.
example: {∅} is not empty: it is a set with one element, and that element is the empty set.

definition: The number of elements in a set, written |A|. For infinite sets, two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection pairs their elements up exactly.

A way to describe a set by a rule instead of listing it: { x ∈ S : condition } means "all x in S for which the condition is true". The colon (or a vertical bar |) is read "such that". It works like a Python set comprehension.
The counting numbers, written ℕ. Authors disagree on whether 0 is included: in computer science ℕ is usually {0, 1, 2, …}, while some maths texts start at 1. Always check the convention.
The whole numbers, positive, negative and zero: {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …}, written ℤ (from the German "Zahlen", numbers).
example: −7, 0 and 42 are integers; 2.5 is not.

definition: Numbers that can be written as a fraction p/q of two integers with q ≠ 0, written ℚ (for "quotient"). Surprisingly, there are only countably many of them.
example: 3/4, −2 (= −2/1) and 0.5 (= 1/2) are rational; √2 is not.

definition: All the points on the number line, including irrational numbers such as √2 and π, written ℝ. Cantor showed there are uncountably many of them.
example: −1.5, 0, √2 ≈ 1.414 and π ≈ 3.14159 are all real numbers.

definition: A ∪ B is the set of elements that are in A, in B, or in both. In Python it is a | b; in SQL it corresponds to UNION.
A ∩ B is the set of elements that are in both A and B. In Python it is a & b.
A ∖ B (also written A \ B or A − B) is the set of elements in A that are not in B. In Python it is a - b.
The set of elements that are in exactly one of two sets: in A or in B but not in both. It is often written A ⊕ B or A △ B, and in Python it is a ^ b.
example: {1, 2, 3, 4} symmetric difference {3, 4, 5} = {1, 2, 5}.

definition: The complement of A is everything in the chosen universe U that is not in A, written Aᶜ (or A′, or with a bar over A). It only makes sense once U is fixed. In counting, "count the complement" means count what you don't want and subtract from the total.
example: With U = {1, …, 10} and A = the even numbers in U, Aᶜ = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}.

definition: The fixed set U of all objects under discussion. Complements are taken relative to it, so the complement of a set depends on which universe you chose.
example: If U is all users and A is the admins, then Aᶜ is every user who is not an admin.

definition: Two rules for pushing a "not" inside a bracket: the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements. The logic version swaps OR for AND (and AND for OR) when NOT moves inside.
example: NOT (country = 'UK' OR plan = 'free') is the same as country <> 'UK' AND plan <> 'free'.

definition: The set of all subsets of A, including ∅ and A itself, written 𝒫(A) or P(A). If A has n elements, its power set has 2ⁿ, because each element is independently in or out.
example: The power set of {a, b} is {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}: 2² = 4 subsets.

definition: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a from A and b from B. Its size is |A| × |B|. A relational table is a subset of the Cartesian product of its column domains.
Two objects written (a, b) in a definite order, so (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different. Unlike a set, order matters and repeats are allowed: (3, 3) is a valid pair.
An ordered list of a fixed number of items, such as (a, b, c). An ordered pair is a 2-tuple. Order matters and repeats are allowed.
example: A row (42, "Ada", "UK") in a three-column table is a 3-tuple.

definition: An integer whose binary digits are used as on/off flags. Bit i set to 1 means "item i is included", so the integers 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 encode every subset of an n-item set.
example: For items [a, b, c], the mask 5 = binary 101 means the subset {a, c}.

definition: A binary digit: a single 0 or 1, the smallest unit of information. n bits can hold 2ⁿ different values.
example: 8 bits make a byte, which has 2⁸ = 256 possible values.

definition: A group of 8 bits, so one of 2⁸ = 256 values. A byte string is a sequence of bytes, the form data takes on disk or on the network.
example: The letter "A" in UTF-8 is the single byte 0x41 (65).

definition: A rule f : A → B that gives every element of the domain A exactly one output in the codomain B. Two conditions: every input has an output, and no input has two outputs. The arrow → in f : A → B is read "from A to". A program routine is a mathematical function only if its result depends on nothing but its inputs.
example: f(x) = x² from ℤ to ℕ is a function: each integer has exactly one square.

definition: The set A of allowed inputs of a function f : A → B. Every element of the domain must be given exactly one output.
example: For f : {1, 2, 3} → {a, b}, the domain is {1, 2, 3}.

definition: The set B that a function f : A → B is declared to map into. Not every element of the codomain has to be hit; the ones that are hit form the image. Whether f is surjective depends on the codomain you declare.
example: f(x) = x² with codomain ℝ is not surjective, but with codomain [0, ∞) it is.

definition: The set of outputs a function actually produces, f(A) = { f(a) : a ∈ A }. It is always a subset of the codomain and may be smaller. Some books call it the range, but "range" is also used for the codomain, so "image" is clearer.
example: For f(1) = a, f(2) = a with codomain {a, b}, the image is {a}.

definition: A function where different inputs always give different outputs: f(x) = f(y) forces x = y. Also called one-to-one. Between finite sets an injection A → B exists only if |A| ≤ |B|, which is why a hash with fewer outputs than inputs must collide.
example: f(x) = 2x on the integers is injective; f(x) = x² is not, since f(−3) = f(3).

definition: A function that hits every element of its codomain: for every b in B some input a has f(a) = b. Also called onto. Its image equals its codomain.
example: Assigning 5 jobs to 3 servers so every server gets at least one job is a surjection from jobs to servers; there are 150 of them.

definition: A function that is both injective and surjective: every element of the codomain is hit by exactly one input. A bijection has an inverse, and two sets have the same size exactly when a bijection exists between them.
example: A block cipher with a fixed key is a bijection on blocks, so decryption can undo it.

definition: For a bijection f : A → B, the inverse f⁻¹ : B → A sends each output back to the one input that produced it, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. The superscript −1 here means "undo", not "1 divided by".
example: If f(x) = x + 3 on the integers, then f⁻¹(y) = y − 3.

definition: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): apply f first, then g. The small circle ∘ is read "after". Composing two injections gives an injection, and two bijections give a bijection.
example: With f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, (g ∘ f)(3) = g(4) = 8.

definition: If more items than boxes are placed into boxes, some box holds at least two. The general form: N items in k boxes forces some box to hold at least ⌈N/k⌉ items (N/k rounded up). It proves collisions must exist without saying where.
example: 1,000,000 keys in 4,096 buckets force some bucket to hold at least ⌈244.14⌉ = 245 keys.

definition: Two different inputs that a hash function maps to the same output. When there are more possible inputs than outputs, the pigeonhole principle says collisions must exist; good hash design only makes them rare or hard to find.
example: Any function from 64-bit IDs to 32-bit slots has collisions, for example many pairs of IDs share a slot.

definition: One slot of a hash table. A key goes into the bucket chosen by its hash value; keys that land in the same bucket have collided.
example: With 4,096 buckets, a key whose hash is 10,000 goes to bucket 10,000 mod 4,096 = 1,808.

definition: A widely used cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family, standardised by NIST in FIPS 180-4. It accepts messages shorter than 2⁶⁴ bits and outputs 256 bits, so collisions must exist, but finding one is believed to be infeasible.
example: sha256(b"abc") begins with ba7816bf…

definition: A set that is finite or can be put in a bijection with the natural numbers, so its elements can be listed in a sequence that eventually reaches each one.
example: The integers are countable: 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, … lists them all.

definition: An infinite set too big to be listed as a sequence: no bijection with the natural numbers exists. The real numbers and the set of all infinite binary sequences are uncountable.
example: Cantor's diagonal argument shows the infinite binary sequences are uncountable.

definition: Georg Cantor's 1891 proof technique: given any list of infinite sequences, build a new sequence that differs from the i-th one at position i. The new one is missing from the list, so no list can be complete. The same trick proves the halting problem undecidable.
example: If the list starts 01101…, 11000…, 00011…, flipping the diagonal bits gives 101…, which differs from every listed sequence.

definition: For every set A, the power set of A is strictly bigger than A: no function from A onto its power set exists. So there is no largest infinity.
example: For A = {1, 2, 3}: |A| = 3 but its power set has 2³ = 8 elements.

definition: The problem of deciding, for any program and input, whether the program eventually stops. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no program can solve it for all cases, using a diagonal argument.
example: No tool can take every Python script and always correctly say whether it terminates.

definition: An endless list of bits b₁, b₂, b₃, …. Each one is the same thing as a function from ℕ to {0, 1}, or a yes/no answer for every natural number. There are uncountably many.
example: The sequence 1, 0, 1, 0, … answers "is n even?" for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ….

definition: Turning an in-memory value into a sequence of bytes (or text) so it can be stored or sent, and decoding it back later. A lossless round trip, decode(encode(x)) = x, requires the encoder to be injective.
example: json.dumps({"a": 1}) serialises a Python dict to the text {"a": 1}.

definition: Encoding a value and decoding it again to get exactly the original back: decode(encode(x)) = x for every valid x. It forces encode to be injective and decode to be surjective onto the values.
example: Base64-encoding the bytes "hi" gives "aGk=", and decoding "aGk=" gives "hi" again.

definition: A way to encode arbitrary bytes as text using 64 safe characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /), with = for padding. Every 3 bytes become 4 characters. It is defined in RFC 4648.
example: The bytes "hi" encode to "aGk=".

definition: The dominant text encoding for Unicode: each character becomes 1 to 4 bytes, and plain ASCII characters keep their single-byte values. It is defined in RFC 3629.
example: "A" is 1 byte (0x41) and "€" is 3 bytes (0xE2 0x82 0xAC).

definition: A common lossless compression format and tool based on the DEFLATE algorithm, specified in RFC 1952. Each file carries a header and checksum, so a tiny or random input can come out larger than it went in.
example: gzip -9 on a 1 MB text log typically shrinks it several-fold, but on already-compressed data it can add a few bytes.

definition: A fast lossless compression algorithm and format developed at Facebook (Meta), specified in RFC 8878. Like any lossless compressor, it cannot shrink every input.
example: zstd is used for compressing logs, packages and database pages.

definition: Compression where decompression gives back exactly the original data. The compressor must therefore be injective, and a counting argument shows it cannot make every input shorter.
example: gzip, zstd and PNG are lossless; ordinary JPEG and MP3 are not.

definition: Compression that throws away some detail to save more space, so decompression gives an approximation of the original. Distinct inputs can map to the same output, so it is not injective.
example: Ordinary JPEG photos and MP3 audio use lossy compression.

definition: A family of image compression standards from the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Ordinary (baseline) JPEG is lossy, although the standard also includes lossless modes.
example: Saving a photo as JPEG at quality 80 discards fine detail the eye barely notices.

definition: A lossy audio compression format (MPEG-1/MPEG-2 Audio Layer III). It discards sounds that listeners are unlikely to notice, so the original audio cannot be recovered exactly.
example: A 128 kbit/s MP3 is roughly a tenth the size of CD-quality audio.

definition: A database rule that no two rows may share the same value in the given column(s). Unlike a primary key, it may allow NULLs, and in many databases several rows may hold NULL.
example: UNIQUE(email) stops two accounts registering ada@example.com.

definition: A special marker in SQL meaning "no value" or "unknown". Comparisons with NULL are neither true nor false but unknown, which is why some logic rewrites only hold when there are no NULLs.
example: WHERE country = 'UK' does not select rows whose country is NULL, and nor does WHERE country <> 'UK'.

definition: An SQL join that pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, with no matching condition. It is the database version of the Cartesian product: 3 rows by 4 rows gives 12.
example: SELECT * FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colours lists every size-colour combination.

definition: The part of an SQL query that filters rows: only rows for which the condition is true are kept.
example: SELECT * FROM users WHERE plan = 'free' returns only free-plan users.

definition: An encryption algorithm that transforms fixed-size blocks of data (128 bits for AES) under a key. For each key it is a bijection on blocks, so every ciphertext block decrypts to exactly one plaintext block.
example: AES-128 maps each 128-bit block to another 128-bit block under a 128-bit key.

definition: A routine whose result depends only on its arguments and which has no side effects. It behaves like a mathematical function, which makes it easy to test, memoise and run in parallel.
example: len(s) is pure; random.random() and print(x) are not.

definition: Anything a routine does besides returning a value: printing, writing a file, changing a global, sending a request. A routine with side effects is not pure even if its return value is predictable.
example: A logging call inside a function is a side effect.

definition: Data a routine reads that is not among its explicit arguments, such as a global variable, the clock or a database. If it can change, the same arguments can give different results, so the routine is not a mathematical function of its arguments.
example: time.time() takes no arguments but returns a different value each call.

definition: Python's immutable set type. Because it cannot change, it is hashable, so it can be an element of another set or a dictionary key, which an ordinary set cannot.
example: {frozenset({1, 2}), frozenset({3})} is a valid set of sets.

definition: In Python, an object with a hash value that never changes during its lifetime and that can be compared for equality. Only hashable objects can be set elements or dictionary keys, and objects that compare equal must have equal hashes.
example: Ints, strings and tuples of them are hashable; lists and sets are not.

definition: Python's built-in unordered collection of distinct hashable elements. It supports | (union), & (intersection), - (difference), ^ (symmetric difference) and <= (subset test).
Θ(g(n)) means "grows at the same rate as g(n)", up to constant factors, for large n: bounded above and below by constant multiples of g(n). Big-O gives only the upper bound.
example: 3n² + 5n is Θ(n²); it is also O(n³), but not Θ(n³).

definition: A simplifying assumption in algorithm analysis that each basic operation (an addition, a comparison, a bit test) takes one step, however large the numbers. It breaks down when numbers grow very large, as in exact big-integer arithmetic.
example: Under the unit-cost model, adding two 2,048-bit numbers counts as one step.

definition: The cost of an algorithm counted in operations on individual bits, so arithmetic on bigger numbers costs more. It is more realistic than the unit-cost model when numbers grow with the input.
example: Fibonacci numbers F(n) have about 0.69n bits, so even adding two of them costs Θ(n) bit operations.

definition: A set R of ordered pairs: R from A to B is a subset of A × B, and a R b (or (a, b) ∈ R) means a is related to b. A relation on one set A is a subset of A × A. Unlike a function, an element may be related to many others or to none.
example: "Divides" on {1, 2, 3, 4} contains (1, 4), (2, 4) and (2, 2) but not (3, 4).

definition: A relation R on A is reflexive if every element is related to itself: a R a for all a in A. In the matrix view the diagonal is all 1s; in the graph view every vertex has a self-loop.
example: ≤ is reflexive (5 ≤ 5); < is not.

definition: A relation in which no element is related to itself. It is stronger than merely "not reflexive", which only needs one element missing its self-pair.
example: < on integers is irreflexive: 5 < 5 is false.

definition: A relation where a R b always implies b R a: every link goes both ways. Its matrix equals its transpose, and in the graph every edge has a reverse edge.
example: "Is a sibling of" is symmetric; "is a parent of" is not.

definition: A relation where a R b and b R a together force a = b: no two-way links between different elements. It is not the opposite of symmetric; equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric.
example: ≤ is antisymmetric: x ≤ y and y ≤ x imply x = y.

definition: A relation where a R b and b R c imply a R c. In the graph view every two-step path has a direct shortcut edge.
example: < is transitive (1 < 2 and 2 < 3 give 1 < 3); "is a friend of" usually is not.

definition: A statement of the form "if A then B" is vacuously true when A never happens, so there is no case that could break it.
example: < is antisymmetric vacuously: a < b and b < a never both hold, so the rule is never tested.

definition: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. It captures "the same in the way we care about", is often written ~, and splits its set into disjoint equivalence classes.
example: Congruence mod 3 is an equivalence relation with classes {…, 0, 3, 6, …}, {…, 1, 4, 7, …} and {…, 2, 5, 8, …}.

definition: For an equivalence relation ~, the class [a] = { x : x ~ a } is everything equivalent to a. Any two classes are either identical or disjoint, so the classes partition the set.
example: Under congruence mod 4 on {0, …, 11}, [7] = {3, 7, 11}.

definition: A way of splitting a set into non-empty, non-overlapping blocks that together cover every element. Partitions correspond one-to-one with equivalence relations.
example: {{1, 2}, {3}} is a partition of {1, 2, 3}; there are 5 partitions of a 3-element set in total.

definition: Bₙ, the number of ways to partition an n-element set, which also counts its equivalence relations. The sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203 for n = 0, 1, 2, ….
example: B₄ = 15: the set {a, b, c, d} can be partitioned in 15 ways.

definition: a ≡ b (mod n), read "a is congruent to b modulo n", means n divides a − b: a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n. It is an equivalence relation whose classes are the n remainders 0 to n − 1. The symbol ≢ means "not congruent".
example: 17 ≡ 5 (mod 12), because 12 divides 17 − 5 = 12: 17:00 is 5 o'clock.

definition: A data structure that keeps track of a partition into groups while you merge them. find(x) returns a representative of x's group and union(a, b) merges two groups. With path compression and union by rank, each operation takes almost constant amortised time.
example: After union(a, b) and union(b, c), find(a) == find(c).

definition: A greedy algorithm for a minimum spanning tree: sort the edges by weight and add each one unless it would create a cycle. Union-find checks whether the two ends are already in the same component.
example: On 100 vertices Kruskal accepts exactly 99 edges to finish a spanning tree of a connected graph.

definition: Solving equations between type expressions, such as list[α] = list[int], by finding values for the type variables. Type checkers for languages such as ML and Haskell use it to infer types.
example: Unifying (α, int) with (str, β) gives α = str and β = int.

definition: A step in unification that refuses to set a type variable equal to a type containing that same variable, such as α = list[α], which would describe an infinitely nested type.
example: Unifying α with list[α] fails the occurs check.

definition: A special IEEE 754 floating-point value produced by undefined operations such as 0/0 or inf − inf. A NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself, so == on floats is not reflexive.
example: float('nan') == float('nan') is False in Python.

definition: The standard for binary floating-point arithmetic used by almost all hardware and languages. It defines formats such as 64-bit doubles and special values such as infinity and NaN.
example: A Python float is an IEEE 754 64-bit double with about 15–17 significant decimal digits.

definition: A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, often written ≼ (read "precedes or equals"). "Partial" means some pairs may be incomparable.
example: ⊆ on subsets is a partial order: {1} and {2} are incomparable.

definition: A set together with a partial order on it. Posets model dependencies, versions and subset inclusion.
example: The divisors of 12 under "divides" form a poset with least element 1 and greatest element 12.

definition: Two elements a and b of a partial order are incomparable when neither a ≼ b nor b ≼ a. Comparable means one of the two does hold.
example: Under "divides", 4 and 6 are incomparable: neither divides the other.

definition: A partial order in which every pair of elements is comparable, so the elements can be laid out in one line. Sorting needs a total order (or a total preorder, which allows ties).
example: ≤ on integers and alphabetical order on strings are total orders.

definition: Like a total order but allowing ties: every pair is comparable and the relation is transitive, but two different items may rank equal. It is what a sort key defines.
example: Sorting people by age is a total preorder: two 30-year-olds tie.

definition: An irreflexive, transitive relation, written ≺ or <. You get one from a partial order ≼ by removing the pairs (a, a). It is automatically antisymmetric.
example: < on integers is the strict order that matches ≤.

definition: a | b, read "a divides b", means b = k × a for some integer k: b is a multiple of a and a is a divisor of b. On positive integers it is a partial order.
example: 3 | 12 because 12 = 4 × 3, but 5 does not divide 12.

definition: A drawing of a finite poset that omits self-loops and any edge implied by transitivity, with larger elements placed higher. You read a ≼ b when there is an upward path from a to b.
example: The Hasse diagram of the subsets of {a, b} is a diamond: ∅ at the bottom, {a, b} at the top.

definition: In a poset, a minimal element has nothing strictly below it; a maximal element has nothing strictly above it. A poset can have several of each.
example: In {2, 3, …, 12} under "divides", the minimal elements are the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.

definition: An element below every other element of the poset; a greatest element is above every other. There is at most one of each, and a least element is also the only minimal element.
example: 1 is the least element of the positive integers under "divides", because 1 divides everything.

definition: A subset of a poset in which every two elements are comparable, so it is totally ordered.
example: {1, 2, 4, 12} is a chain under "divides": 1 | 2 | 4 | 12.

definition: A subset of a poset in which no two different elements are comparable.
example: {4, 6} is an antichain under "divides".

definition: An upper bound of a and b is an element at or above both; the least upper bound, or join, is the smallest such element. The greatest lower bound, or meet, is defined the other way round.
example: In the subset order, the join of {1} and {2} is {1, 2} and the meet is ∅.

definition: The largest element that is at or below both a and b in a poset. In the subset order the meet of two sets is their intersection.
example: Under "divides", the meet of 12 and 18 is their gcd, 6.

definition: A poset in which every pair of elements has both a join (least upper bound) and a meet (greatest lower bound). A join-semilattice only guarantees joins. State-based CRDTs merge replicas by taking joins.
example: The subsets of a set form a lattice with union as join and intersection as meet.

definition: A data type designed so replicas can be updated independently and then merged without conflicts. State-based CRDTs merge with a join on a semilattice; operation-based CRDTs instead rely on delivery and commutativity guarantees.
example: A grow-only counter keeps one count per replica and merges by taking the maximum of each.

definition: A total order that respects a given partial order: whenever a ≺ b in the partial order, a comes before b. A topological sort produces one.
example: utils, config, lib, app is a linear extension of the build dependency order.

definition: An ordering of the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that every edge goes from earlier to later. It exists exactly when there is no cycle, and runs in O(n + m) with Kahn's algorithm or depth-first search.
example: Builds compile utils before lib before app because of a topological sort of their dependencies.

definition: A directed graph with no directed cycles. Its reachability relation is a strict partial order, so it can always be topologically sorted.
example: Package dependencies, build steps and git commit history are usually DAGs.

definition: Having no cycles. An undirected acyclic graph is a forest; a connected one is a tree. A directed acyclic graph is a DAG.
example: A family tree drawn parent-to-child is acyclic.

definition: A Python standard-library module (since 3.9) whose TopologicalSorter class topologically sorts a dependency graph and raises CycleError if there is a cycle.
example: TopologicalSorter({"b": {"a"}}).static_order() yields a then b.

definition: The standard package installer for Python. It resolves a package's dependencies and installs them.
example: pip install requests also installs the packages requests depends on.

definition: A list of counters, one per participant, attached to each event or version. V ≤ W when every counter in V is ≤ the matching one in W; if neither holds, the two are concurrent. This comparison is a partial order.
example: [2, 1, 0] and [1, 2, 0] are concurrent; [2, 2, 1] descends from both.

definition: Two events or versions where neither happened before the other in the causal order: they are incomparable. Their updates may conflict and need merging.
example: Two users editing the same key on different replicas without seeing each other's write create concurrent versions.

definition: Leslie Lamport's 1978 logical clock: a single counter per process, bumped on each event and on receiving a message. If a happened before b, then a's timestamp is smaller, but a smaller timestamp does not prove causality.
example: Breaking ties by process ID turns Lamport timestamps into a total order.

definition: A distributed key-value store modelled on Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper, such as Riak. It replicates data across nodes, accepts writes during failures and can keep concurrent versions (siblings) for the application to merge.
example: Riak returns two sibling values when two clients write the same key concurrently.

definition: The smallest transitive relation that contains R: a R⁺ b when there is a path of one or more R-steps from a to b. It answers "can a reach b, directly or indirectly?".
example: For edges 1→2 and 2→3, the transitive closure adds 1→3.

definition: The smallest reflexive relation containing R: add every self-pair (a, a).
example: The reflexive closure of < is ≤.

definition: The smallest symmetric relation containing R: add the reverse (b, a) of every pair (a, b).
example: The symmetric closure of "follows" is "follows or is followed by".

definition: An algorithm that computes the transitive closure of a relation on n elements from its adjacency matrix in O(n³) time, by allowing each element in turn as an intermediate stop.
example: For n = 1,000 that is about 10⁹ basic steps.

definition: An n × n grid of 0s and 1s where the entry in row u, column v is 1 when u is related (or joined by an edge) to v. It checks an edge in O(1) but always uses O(n²) space.
example: A graph with 10,000 vertices needs 10⁸ cells, even if it has only 20,000 edges.

definition: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours. It uses O(n + m) space, so it suits sparse graphs.
example: {"a": ["b", "c"], "b": ["a"], "c": ["a"]} is an adjacency list.

definition: The matrix obtained by swapping rows and columns: entry (i, j) becomes entry (j, i). A relation is symmetric exactly when its matrix equals its transpose.
An SQL query (WITH RECURSIVE …) that repeatedly joins its own result with a table until nothing new appears. It is how SQL computes reachability, such as everyone above an employee in an org chart.
example: A recursive CTE over a deps table lists every package an app depends on, directly or indirectly.

definition: A function a sort calls to decide which of two items comes first. Sorting only behaves predictably if the comparator is consistent: transitive and describing a total preorder.
example: A comparator in which rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper and paper beats rock has a cycle and cannot be sorted by.

definition: A hybrid merge sort and insertion sort designed by Tim Peters for Python in 2002, and used by Java for sorting objects. Java's version may throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!" when it detects an inconsistent comparator.
example: Python 3.11 kept TimSort for list.sort() but replaced its rule for choosing which runs to merge with the one from powersort.

definition: An edge from a vertex to itself. In the graph picture of a relation, a self-loop on a means a R a. Simple graphs do not allow them.
example: A reflexive relation on {1, 2, 3} draws as a graph with a self-loop on each of the three vertices.

definition: If a task is a sequence of steps with a choices for the first and b for the second (whatever the first was), there are a × b ways in total.
example: A 4-digit PIN has 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10,000 possibilities.

definition: If a task can be done in one of several disjoint (non-overlapping) ways, the total is the sum of the counts. Overlapping cases need inclusion–exclusion instead.
example: Passwords of length 1, 2 or 3 over a–z: 26 + 676 + 17,576 = 18,278.

definition: An ordering of a set of items, or a bijection from a set to itself. n distinct items have n! permutations.
example: abc, acb, bac, bca, cab and cba are the 3! = 6 permutations of a, b, c.

definition: n! ("n factorial") is n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1, the number of orderings of n distinct items. By convention 0! = 1. It eventually grows faster than any exponential cⁿ with a fixed base c.
P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)! counts ordered selections of k distinct items from n: n choices, then n − 1, down to n − k + 1. Python computes it as math.perm(n, k).
example: Gold, silver and bronze from 8 runners: P(8, 3) = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336.

definition: A selection where order does not matter, which is a subset. The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is the binomial coefficient C(n, k).
example: Choosing a team of 3 from 8 people: C(8, 3) = 56 combinations.

definition: C(n, k), read "n choose k" and also written as n over k in tall brackets, is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set: n! / (k! × (n − k)!). Python computes it as math.comb(n, k).
example: C(5, 2) = 10: there are 10 ways to pick 2 items from 5.

definition: C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k): fix one item; each subset either contains it or doesn't. Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it.
A triangle of numbers where row n lists C(n, 0), C(n, 1), …, C(n, n) and each entry is the sum of the two above it. Row n adds up to 2ⁿ.
example: Row 4 is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, which sums to 16 = 2⁴.

definition: The rule for expanding (x + y)ⁿ: the coefficient of xᵏ yⁿ⁻ᵏ is C(n, k), because it counts the ways to pick x from k of the n brackets.
example: (x + y)³ = x³ + 3x²y + 3xy² + y³.

definition: A route on a grid of integer points that moves one unit at a time, here only right or up. Paths from (0, 0) to (a, b) number C(a + b, b), because you choose which of the a + b steps go up.
example: From (0, 0) to (4, 3) there are C(7, 3) = 35 such paths.

definition: A collection where order does not matter but repeats are allowed. Choosing k items from n kinds with repetition gives C(n + k − 1, k) multisets.
example: {1, 1, 2} is a multiset of size 3; it differs from {1, 2}.

definition: A counting trick: distributing k identical items into n distinct bins is the same as arranging k stars and n − 1 bars in a row, giving C(n + k − 1, n − 1) ways (which equals C(n + k − 1, k)).
example: 10 identical jobs to 4 workers: C(13, 3) = 286 ways.

definition: The number of ways to arrange n items when there are groups of identical items: n! divided by the factorial of each group size. It generalises the binomial coefficient to more than two groups.
example: BANANA (A × 3, N × 2, B × 1) has 6! / (3! × 2! × 1!) = 60 arrangements.

definition: A Python standard-library module of fast iterator building blocks, including permutations, combinations and product for brute-force enumeration.
example: list(itertools.combinations("abc", 2)) gives [("a","b"), ("a","c"), ("b","c")].

definition: ⌈x⌉ is the smallest integer greater than or equal to x: x rounded up. Rounding up to a multiple of m gives m × ⌈x / m⌉, the smallest multiple of m that is at least x. It appears in the generalised pigeonhole principle.
⌊x⌋ is the largest integer less than or equal to x: x rounded down, towards minus infinity. Python's // operator does floor division.
Solving a problem by trying every possibility. Counting tells you how many there are, and so whether brute force is feasible.
example: Trying all 10,000 four-digit PINs is easy; trying all 62¹² 12-character passwords is not.

definition: The set of all candidate answers a search may have to try. Its size, found by counting, bounds how long brute force can take.
example: An 8-character password over 62 symbols has a search space of 62⁸ ≈ 2.18 × 10¹⁴.

definition: Find the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns home. Trying every order costs about n! tours; the decision version ("is there a tour of cost at most B?") is NP-complete.
example: 20 cities have 19!/2 ≈ 6 × 10¹⁶ distinct tours.

definition: A sorting algorithm that learns about the order only by comparing pairs of items. It must tell apart all n! orderings, so in the worst case it needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons, which grows like n log₂ n (for 20 items, log₂(20!) ≈ 61).
example: Merge sort, heapsort and TimSort are comparison sorts; counting sort is not.

definition: log₂ x is the power you raise 2 to in order to get x, so log₂ 8 = 3. It counts how many times you can halve x before reaching 1, which is why it appears in binary search and divide-and-conquer.
ln x is the logarithm to base e ≈ 2.71828. It appears in the prime number theorem: about n / ln n numbers up to n are prime.

How many random items until a repeat becomes likely? With 365 equally likely birthdays, 23 people give a better than 50% chance of a shared birthday. For b-bit hash outputs collisions become likely around 2^(b/2) items.
example: A 32-bit hash is expected to collide after roughly 2¹⁶ ≈ 65,000 random inputs.

definition: Every possible value is equally likely. Independent and uniform means each choice is equally likely and unaffected by the others, which is the assumption behind most counting-based security estimates.
example: A fair die gives each of 1–6 with probability 1/6.

definition: A unit of 1,024 bytes (2¹⁰), from the IEC binary prefixes. 1 KiB is 8,192 bits.
example: A 1 KiB file has 2⁸¹⁹² possible contents.

definition: A short numeric code used to authenticate, such as a 4-digit card or door code.
example: A 4-digit PIN has 10⁴ = 10,000 possible values.

definition: An ordering around a circle where rotations count as the same. n distinct people have (n − 1)! circular arrangements; if mirror images also count as the same (and n ≥ 3), there are (n − 1)!/2.
example: 6 people round a table: 5! = 120 seatings.

definition: Counting what you want by counting everything and subtracting what you don't want. It is the fastest route for "at least one" conditions.
example: Codes of 6 characters over a–z, 0–9 with at least one digit: 36⁶ − 26⁶ = 1,867,866,560.

definition: Counting some objects more than once, as when a retried or replayed event is tallied twice. In combinatorics it is fixed by dividing out a known repetition factor (as C(n, k) = P(n, k) / k! does) or by inclusion–exclusion.
example: Counting committees of 3 as ordered triples counts each committee 3! = 6 times.

definition: A formula for the size of a union of overlapping sets: add the sizes of the sets, subtract the sizes of all pairwise intersections, add the triple intersections, and so on, alternating.
example: |A ∪ B| = 18 + 15 − 8 = 25 when 18 know Python, 15 know Java and 8 know both.

definition: Sets with no element in common: their intersection is empty. The sum rule only works for disjoint cases.
example: {1, 2} and {3, 4} are disjoint; {1, 2} and {2, 3} are not.

definition: A permutation in which no item stays in its original position (it has no fixed point). D(n) is the nearest integer to n!/e for n ≥ 1, so about 36.8% of large random permutations are derangements.
example: D(4) = 9: 4 people can swap coats so nobody gets their own in 9 ways.

definition: The mathematical constant e ≈ 2.71828, the base of natural logarithms. 1/e ≈ 0.368 appears as the limit of the fraction of permutations that are derangements.
example: 4!/e ≈ 8.83, which rounds to D(4) = 9.

definition: An infinite sum a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + …. In counting it is used "formally": nobody plugs in a value for x, the coefficients simply store a sequence.
example: 1 + x + x² + x³ + … is the power series of 1/(1 − x).

definition: An equation that defines each term of a sequence from earlier terms, plus base cases to start it. It describes the running time of recursive code and the counts that dynamic programming computes.
The starting values of a recurrence or recursion, given directly instead of from earlier terms. The same recurrence with different base cases gives a different sequence.
example: a(n) = a(n − 1) + a(n − 2) with a(0) = 0, a(1) = 1 gives Fibonacci; with a(0) = 2, a(1) = 1 it gives the Lucas numbers.

definition: The sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … where each term is the sum of the two before: F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2) with F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1. It grows like φⁿ/√5 with φ ≈ 1.618.
The sequence 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, … that follows the Fibonacci rule but starts from L(0) = 2 and L(1) = 1. It shows how base cases change a recurrence's values.
A puzzle: move a stack of n discs between three pegs, one disc at a time, never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. The minimum number of moves obeys T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 and equals 2ⁿ − 1.
example: 10 discs need 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1,023 moves.

definition: A proof method for statements about every natural number: prove the base case, then prove that if the statement holds for n − 1 it also holds for n. It is the standard way to confirm a guessed closed form for a recurrence.
A formula that computes the n-th term directly, with a fixed number of standard operations, instead of from earlier terms.
example: T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1 is the closed form of the Tower of Hanoi recurrence.

aliases: linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients
definition: A recurrence where each term is a fixed weighted sum of a fixed number of earlier terms, with no extra added term: a(n) = c₁ × a(n − 1) + c₂ × a(n − 2) is second-order. It is solved with the characteristic equation.
example: a(n) = 5a(n − 1) − 6a(n − 2) is linear, homogeneous and second-order.

definition: The polynomial equation you get by trying a(n) = rⁿ in a linear recurrence. For a(n) = c₁ a(n − 1) + c₂ a(n − 2) it is r² = c₁ r + c₂, and its roots give the growth rates in the solution.
example: For a(n) = 5a(n − 1) − 6a(n − 2) it is r² − 5r + 6 = 0, with roots 2 and 3.

definition: A root that appears more than once in a polynomial, as 2 does in (r − 2)² = 0. For a recurrence with a double root r ≠ 0, the solution is (α + βn) × rⁿ.
example: a(n) = 4a(n − 1) − 4a(n − 2) has the double root 2.

definition: φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618, the larger root of r² = r + 1. Fibonacci numbers grow like φⁿ/√5. (In number theory, φ is used for Euler's totient instead; the two are unrelated.)
Short for dynamic programming: solving a problem by building up and storing answers to smaller subproblems, often by filling a table in a fixed order.
example: The coin-change DP fills a list with the number of ways to make every amount from 0 up to n pence.

definition: An algorithm design that splits a problem into smaller copies, solves them recursively and combines the results. Its running time satisfies T(n) = a × T(n/b) + f(n).
example: Merge sort splits a list in two, sorts each half and merges them.

definition: A divide-and-conquer sort: split the list in half, sort each half, then merge them. Its running time obeys T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n and is Θ(n log n).
example: Sorting 1,024 items takes about 10 levels of merging, each touching all 1,024 items.

definition: A theorem that solves many divide-and-conquer recurrences T(n) = a × T(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a), the work at the leaves. If one grows polynomially faster it dominates (with a regularity condition when f(n) wins); if they match, an extra log factor appears.
example: For merge sort, a = b = 2 and f(n) = n = n^(log₂ 2), so T(n) = Θ(n log n).

definition: Anatoly Karatsuba's 1960 divide-and-conquer method that multiplies two n-digit numbers with three half-size multiplications instead of four, giving O(n^1.585) instead of O(n²).
example: Python uses Karatsuba for multiplying very large integers.

definition: A simple Θ(n²) sort that repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and moves it to the front. Its running time obeys T(n) = T(n − 1) + n.
example: Sorting 1,000 items takes about 500,000 comparisons.

definition: A divide-and-conquer sort that partitions around a pivot and recurses on each side. It averages Θ(n log n) but degrades to Θ(n²) when pivots are consistently extreme.
example: Choosing the first element as pivot on an already-sorted list gives the Θ(n²) worst case.

definition: A power series A(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + … whose coefficients are a sequence of counts. Multiplying two generating functions combines independent choices, turning counting into algebra.
example: The coefficient of xⁿ in 1/((1 − x)(1 − x²)(1 − x⁵)) counts the ways to make n pence from 1p, 2p and 5p coins.

definition: The way two sequences combine when their generating functions are multiplied: the n-th term is the sum of aᵢ × bₙ₋ᵢ over all splits of n into i and n − i.
example: Convolving 1, 1, 1, … with itself gives 1, 2, 3, …: the number of ways to split n into two parts.

definition: A sum where each term is a fixed multiple of the one before: 1 + x + x² + x³ + …. As a formal power series it equals 1/(1 − x).
The number multiplying a power of a variable in an expression. In a generating function, the coefficient of xⁿ is the count you want.
example: In 3x² + 5x + 1, the coefficient of x² is 3.

definition: An expression built from a variable using addition and multiplication by constants, such as 3x² + 5x + 1. Its degree is its highest power. In complexity theory, a polynomial bound such as n³ is what separates efficient (polynomial-time) algorithms from exponential ones.
example: r² − 5r + 6 is a polynomial of degree 2 with roots 2 and 3.

definition: Counting (or minimising) the ways to make an amount from given coin denominations. Looping over coins on the outside counts each combination of coins once, ignoring order.
example: With 1p, 2p and 5p coins there are 10 ways to make 10p.

definition: Rewriting a fraction of polynomials as a sum of simpler fractions such as A/(1 − r x). Each simple fraction expands into a geometric series, which yields closed forms.
example: 1/((1 − x)(1 − 2x)) = 2/(1 − 2x) − 1/(1 − x), so its coefficients are 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1.

definition: The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, … with C(n) = C(2n, n)/(n + 1). They count balanced bracket strings, binary-tree shapes and polygon triangulations.
example: There are C(3) = 5 balanced strings of 3 bracket pairs: ((())), (()()), (())(), ()(()), ()()().

definition: A way to cut a convex polygon into triangles using diagonals that do not cross. A polygon with n + 2 vertices has C(n) triangulations (the n-th Catalan number).
example: A hexagon (6 = 4 + 2 vertices) has C(4) = 14 triangulations.

definition: A proposed set of code changes submitted for review before being merged into a shared repository.
example: An engineer opens a pull request, a teammate reviews it, and it is merged.

definition: A structure G = (V, E): a set V of vertices (points) and a set E of edges joining pairs of them. It models anything made of things and connections, such as roads, networks and dependencies.
example: A triangle is the graph with V = {a, b, c} and E = {{a, b}, {b, c}, {a, c}}.

definition: One of the points of a graph, also called a node. The set of vertices is written V, and n = |V| is usually the number of them.
example: In a road network, each junction is a vertex.

definition: A connection between two vertices of a graph. In an undirected graph it is an unordered pair {u, v}; in a directed graph it is an ordered pair (u, v). The set of edges is written E and m = |E| is usually the number of them.
example: A road between two junctions is an edge.

definition: A graph whose edges have no direction: an edge {u, v} lets you go either way.
example: A Facebook-style friendship network is undirected.

definition: A graph whose edges are ordered pairs (u, v), drawn as arrows from u to v.
example: A "follows" network is directed: you can follow someone who doesn't follow you.

definition: A graph with no self-loops and at most one edge between any two vertices.
example: K₄ is simple; a graph with two edges between the same pair is a multigraph.

definition: A graph that may have several edges between the same pair of vertices.
example: Königsberg, with two bridges between some land masses, is a multigraph.

definition: The number of edges touching a vertex, written deg(v); a self-loop counts twice. The degrees always add up to twice the number of edges.
example: In a triangle every vertex has degree 2, and 2 + 2 + 2 = 2 × 3.

definition: In a directed graph, a vertex's in-degree is the number of edges arriving and its out-degree the number leaving.
example: If a follows b and c, and nobody follows a, then a has out-degree 2 and in-degree 0.

definition: Δ(G), the largest vertex degree in a graph G. Greedy colouring never needs more than Δ + 1 colours.
example: A star with 100 leaves has Δ = 100.

definition: A sequence of vertices where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge. Vertices and edges may repeat. A closed walk ends where it started.
example: a, b, a, c is a walk in the triangle a, b, c.

definition: A walk that repeats no vertex. A path of length k uses k edges; a zero-length path is a single vertex.
example: a, b, c is a path of length 2 in the triangle a, b, c.

definition: A walk that never reuses an edge, although it may revisit vertices. An Euler trail is a trail that uses every edge.
example: In a bowtie graph you can trace all 6 edges as one closed trail through the centre twice.

definition: A closed path: it returns to its start without repeating any other vertex, and has at least 3 vertices in a simple graph. Cₙ is the graph that is a single cycle on n vertices. An odd cycle has an odd number of vertices.
example: C₅ is a pentagon; it is an odd cycle and needs 3 colours.

definition: An undirected graph in which there is a path between every pair of vertices.
example: A tree is connected; two separate triangles drawn side by side are not.

definition: A maximal group of vertices that are all joined to each other by paths. "Is connected to" is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the components.
example: A forest with 100 vertices and 93 edges has 7 connected components.

definition: Kₙ, the simple graph on n vertices with an edge between every pair: n(n − 1)/2 edges. Every vertex has degree n − 1.
example: A full mesh of 10 servers is K₁₀, with 45 links.

definition: The complete graph on 5 vertices, with 10 edges. It is the smallest complete graph that cannot be drawn in the plane without crossings.
example: K₅ has 10 edges, more than the 3 × 5 − 6 = 9 any simple planar graph on 5 vertices can have.

definition: The complete bipartite graph with two sides of 3 vertices, every vertex on one side joined to every vertex on the other: 9 edges. It is not planar, which is the classic "three houses, three utilities" puzzle.
example: K₃,₃ has 6 vertices and 9 edges but 2 × 6 − 4 = 8, so it cannot be planar.

definition: In any graph the degrees add up to twice the number of edges, because each edge has two ends. So the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.
example: No graph has 7 vertices all of degree 3: the sum would be 21, which is odd.

definition: A graph with far fewer edges than the maximum n(n − 1)/2, typically m about proportional to n. A dense graph has m close to n². Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; matrices suit dense ones.
example: A road map with 10⁶ junctions and 2.5 × 10⁶ roads is sparse.

definition: A connected graph with no cycles. A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and exactly one simple path between any two vertices.
example: An org chart of 50 people is a tree with 49 reporting lines.

definition: A graph with no cycles, not necessarily connected: a collection of trees. A forest with n vertices and m edges has exactly n − m components.
example: Kruskal's algorithm grows a forest until it becomes one spanning tree.

definition: A tree that uses all the vertices of a connected graph and some of its edges. Every connected graph has one.
example: A spanning tree of K₄ uses all 4 vertices and 3 of its 6 edges.

definition: An Ethernet network protocol, standardised in IEEE 802.1D, that switches run to agree on a spanning tree of the links and block the rest, so broadcast frames cannot loop forever.
example: Two switches joined by two cables would loop broadcasts without STP disabling one link.

definition: A broadcast message endlessly circulating round a cycle of network links, multiplying until it swamps the network.
example: Plugging both ends of a cable into the same unmanaged switch can cause a broadcast storm.

definition: The dominant family of wired local-network technologies (IEEE 802.3). Switches forward Ethernet frames between devices.
example: An office LAN with switches and RJ45 cables is Ethernet.

definition: The number of different trees on n labelled vertices is nⁿ⁻² (for n ≥ 2).
example: On 4 labelled vertices there are 4² = 16 trees.

definition: The 1736 puzzle that started graph theory: could you walk through Königsberg crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once? Euler proved you couldn't, because all four land masses had odd degree.
example: The land masses had degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3: four odd vertices, so no Euler path.

definition: A closed walk that uses every edge exactly once. A graph whose edge-bearing vertices are all connected has one exactly when every vertex has even degree.
example: A square (C₄) has an Euler circuit: go round it once.

definition: A walk that uses every edge exactly once, not necessarily ending where it started. In a connected graph it exists exactly when 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree; with 2, it must start at one and end at the other.
example: Adding one bridge between two degree-3 land masses of Königsberg leaves two odd vertices, so an Euler path appears.

definition: Euler's 1736 result, completed by Hierholzer in 1873: a connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree, and an Euler path if and only if 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. Not to be confused with Euler's theorem in number theory.
example: A graph with degrees 2, 4, 3, 3, 2 has an Euler path between the two degree-3 vertices.

definition: Carl Hierholzer's linear-time method for constructing an Euler circuit: follow unused edges until you return to the start, then splice in further loops from vertices that still have unused edges. It runs in O(m).
example: On a graph with 1,000 edges it does work proportional to 1,000.

definition: A directed graph whose vertices are short strings and whose edges join strings that overlap by all but one character. Euler paths through it reassemble DNA from overlapping fragments and generate de Bruijn sequences.
example: In genome assembly, reads are cut into overlapping k-mers that become the edges of a de Bruijn graph.

definition: A shortest cyclic string over an alphabet of k symbols in which every possible string of length n appears exactly once as a window: length kⁿ. It comes from an Euler circuit of a de Bruijn graph.
example: For bits and n = 2, 0011 (read cyclically) contains 00, 01, 11 and 10.

definition: Find the shortest closed route that travels every edge at least once. If the graph has an Euler circuit, that is the answer; otherwise some edges must be repeated. It is solvable in polynomial time.
example: Planning a snowplough or postal route that covers every street is a Chinese postman problem.

definition: A cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start (a Hamiltonian path need not return). Deciding whether one exists is NP-complete, unlike the linear-time Euler-circuit test.
example: A cycle C₆ is itself a Hamiltonian cycle; the bowtie graph has none.

definition: An algorithm runs in polynomial time if its steps grow at most like a fixed power of the input size, such as n² or n³. It is the usual formal meaning of "efficient".
example: Checking every vertex degree is O(n + m), which is polynomial; trying all n! orderings is not.

definition: Running time proportional to the input size; for a graph, O(n + m): a constant amount of work per vertex and per edge.
example: Counting the odd-degree vertices of a graph takes linear time.

definition: A sufficient condition guarantees the result; a necessary condition must hold for the result to be possible. Dirac's theorem is sufficient but not necessary for a Hamiltonian cycle.
example: C₁₀ has degree 2 < 10/2 everywhere yet is Hamiltonian: Dirac's condition is not necessary.

definition: Gabriel Dirac's 1952 result: a simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices in which every vertex has degree at least n/2 has a Hamiltonian cycle.
example: A graph on 10 vertices with every degree at least 5 is guaranteed a Hamiltonian cycle.

definition: Two triangles sharing one vertex: 5 vertices and 6 edges. All degrees are even (2 or 4), so it has an Euler circuit, but no Hamiltonian cycle because any tour must pass through the shared vertex twice.
example: Its centre vertex has degree 4; the other four have degree 2.

definition: An assignment of colours to the vertices of a graph so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. It models keeping conflicting things apart.
example: Colouring a 5-cycle A=1, B=2, C=1, D=2, E=3 is proper: no neighbours share a colour.

definition: χ(G), the smallest number of colours that properly colours the graph G. χ is the Greek letter chi.
example: χ(Kₙ) = n, χ of an even cycle is 2 and χ of an odd cycle is 3.

definition: A graph whose vertices split into two sides so that every edge goes between the sides: exactly the 2-colourable graphs. A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle.
example: Trees and even cycles are bipartite; a triangle is not.

definition: Whether a graph can be properly coloured with 3 colours. Deciding it is NP-complete, even though 2-colourability is linear-time.
example: An odd cycle is 3-colourable but K₄ is not.

definition: Colouring vertices one by one, giving each the smallest colour not used by its already-coloured neighbours. It uses at most Δ + 1 colours, but a bad order can use far more than the chromatic number.
example: On a bipartite "crown" graph a bad order can force about n/2 colours where 2 suffice.

definition: The compiler step that decides which variables live in CPU registers at each point. Chaitin's method colours the interference graph, with one colour per register.
example: With 16 registers, a program whose interference graph needs 17 colours must spill or split something.

definition: A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the processor that instructions operate on directly. There are only a handful, for example 16 general-purpose registers in x86-64.
example: Adding two numbers usually means loading them into registers first.

definition: A graph with a vertex per variable and an edge between two variables that are live at the same time, so they cannot share a register.
example: Four values all live at once form K₄ and need 4 registers.

definition: The stretch of a program during which a variable holds a value that will still be read later. Variables whose live ranges overlap interfere.
example: In x = 1; y = x + 2; print(y), x is live only until y is computed.

definition: Storing a variable in memory instead of a register, loading it back when needed. It frees a register at the cost of slower memory accesses.
example: With 3 registers and 4 values live at once, the compiler spills one value to the stack.

definition: Recomputing a value when it is needed instead of keeping it in a register or spilling it, when recomputing is cheap.
example: A constant like 42 can be reloaded with one instruction instead of occupying a register.

definition: Every planar graph can be properly coloured with at most 4 colours. Appel and Haken proved it in 1976 with a large computer-checked case analysis.
example: Any map of countries (each a connected region) can be coloured with 4 colours so neighbours differ.

definition: A graph that can be drawn on a flat surface with no edges crossing; such a drawing is a plane graph. Simple planar graphs with V ≥ 3 have at most 3V − 6 edges.
example: A cube's skeleton is planar; K₅ and K₃,₃ are not.

definition: A region of the plane bounded by edges of a planar drawing, including the unbounded outer region.
example: A drawing of a cube has 6 faces: 5 inner regions and the outside.

definition: For a connected planar drawing, V − E + F = 2, where V, E and F count vertices, edges and faces (including the outer face).
Kazimierz Kuratowski's 1930 theorem: a graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃.
example: The Petersen graph contains a subdivision of K₃,₃, so it is not planar.

definition: A graph made by inserting new degree-2 vertices along edges, turning an edge into a path. It does not change whether the graph can be drawn without crossings.
example: Putting a midpoint on every edge of K₅ gives a subdivision of K₅ with 15 vertices.

definition: A board that holds and wires electronic components with copper tracks. Tracks on one layer cannot cross, so non-planar connections need extra layers or jumpers.
example: A 4-layer PCB has copper tracks on four stacked layers.

definition: Edsger Dijkstra's 1959 algorithm for shortest paths from one vertex in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
example: Route planners use variants of Dijkstra to find the fastest road route.

definition: A directed graph with a vertex per function in a program and an edge from f to g when f calls g.
example: A profiler can draw a call graph showing main calling parse and render.

definition: Whether an integer is even or odd. Colouring vertices by the parity of their distance from a start vertex is how BFS tests bipartiteness.
example: Distances 0, 2 and 4 have even parity; 1 and 3 have odd parity.

definition: A tree with one centre vertex joined to every other vertex (the leaves), and no other edges.
example: A star with 100 leaves has 101 vertices, 100 edges and is planar.

definition: The 21 problems Richard Karp showed NP-complete in 1972, including Hamiltonian cycle, graph colouring and clique, which made NP-completeness central to computer science.
example: Directed and undirected Hamiltonian cycle are both on Karp's list.

definition: Arithmetic on remainders: a mod n is the remainder r (0 ≤ r < n) when a is divided by n, and n is the modulus. Numbers "wrap around" after n − 1, as on a clock.
example: 17 mod 5 = 2 and 14:00 + 13 hours on a 24-hour clock is (14 + 13) mod 24 = 3:00.

definition: What is left over after dividing one integer by another: a = q × n + r. In maths r is chosen with 0 ≤ r < n, but some languages return a negative r for negative a.
example: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2, so the remainder of 17 divided by 5 is 2.

definition: The whole number of times n fits into a when dividing: q in a = q × n + r. (In automata, a quotient instead means merging equivalent states into one, as in DFA minimisation.)
example: 17 divided by 5 has quotient 3 and remainder 2.

definition: The fact that for integers a and n > 0 there are unique integers q and r with a = q × n + r and 0 ≤ r < n.
A Python built-in that returns the quotient and remainder together: divmod(a, n) = (a // n, a % n).
example: divmod(17, 5) returns (3, 2) and divmod(-7, 3) returns (-3, 2).

definition: Integer division that drops the fractional part, rounding towards zero. C, C++, Java and Go use it, so the remainder takes the sign of the dividend and can be negative.
example: In Java, -7 / 3 is -2 and -7 % 3 is -1.

definition: A Java method that returns the floored remainder: for a positive modulus n, the result is always in 0 to n − 1, even for negative inputs.
example: Math.floorMod(-7, 3) returns 2, while -7 % 3 returns -1.

definition: When an arithmetic result does not fit in a fixed-width integer type. Unsigned C/C++ types wrap modulo 2ᵏ; signed overflow in C/C++ is undefined behaviour; Java wraps signed ints silently.
example: In Java, Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE = −2,147,483,648.

definition: Fixed-width means taking the same number of bits, bytes or characters whatever the value. A fixed-width integer type has a set number of bits, such as 32 or 64, so only a limited range of values fits.
A fixed-width integer type that holds only non-negative values: k bits give 0 to 2ᵏ − 1. In C and C++ its arithmetic wraps modulo 2ᵏ.
example: An 8-bit unsigned 255 + 1 wraps to 0.

definition: Arithmetic that goes past the largest value and comes back round to the smallest, like a clock: the result is reduced modulo 2ᵏ.
example: A 64-bit unsigned counter at 2⁶⁴ − 1 wraps to 0 when incremented.

definition: JavaScript's arbitrary-precision integer type, written with an n suffix (10n). Its division truncates towards zero.
example: -7n / 3n is -2n and -7n % 3n is -1n.

definition: One of the n possible remainders 0, 1, …, n − 1 modulo n, standing for the whole class of integers congruent to it.
example: Modulo 5 there are 5 residues: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; −3 belongs to the residue 2.

definition: gcd(a, b) is the largest positive integer that divides both a and b. By convention gcd(0, 0) = 0 in programming. Euclid's algorithm computes it fast.

The method, from Euclid's Elements around 300 BC, for computing gcd(a, b) by replacing (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until the second number is 0. Its number of steps is at most proportional to the number of digits of the smaller input.
Gabriel Lamé's 1844 result that Euclid's algorithm takes at most about five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller input in steps, with consecutive Fibonacci numbers as the worst case.
example: gcd(89, 55) takes 9 division steps, the most for inputs of that size.

definition: For integers a and b there are integers x and y with a × x + b × y = gcd(a, b). The extended Euclidean algorithm finds x and y, and they give modular inverses.
Euclid's algorithm plus bookkeeping of how each remainder is built from a and b, so it returns gcd(a, b) and Bézout coefficients x and y with a × x + b × y = gcd(a, b).
The maximum depth of nested function calls Python allows (1,000 by default) before raising RecursionError, which protects the C stack from overflowing.
example: sys.getrecursionlimit() returns 1000 in a default CPython.

definition: A number a⁻¹ with a × a⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n). It exists exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1, and it is how you "divide by a" in modular arithmetic. Python finds it with pow(a, -1, n).
example: The inverse of 7 mod 40 is 23, because 7 × 23 = 161 = 4 × 40 + 1.

definition: Two integers are coprime when their only positive common divisor is 1: gcd(a, b) = 1.
example: 8 and 15 are coprime; 8 and 12 are not (both are divisible by 4).

definition: A finite set with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by non-zero elements, all obeying the usual laws. The integers mod a prime p form one; GF(2⁸) is another, with 256 elements.
example: Mod 7, every non-zero residue has an inverse, e.g. 3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1.

definition: The finite field with 256 elements, each stored as a byte. Addition is XOR and multiplication is polynomial multiplication reduced by a fixed polynomial, not ordinary arithmetic mod 256. AES and many Reed–Solomon codes use it.
example: In GF(2⁸), 0x53 + 0xCA = 0x99 (XOR).

definition: Public-key cryptography built on the group of points of an elliptic curve over a finite field. It gives security comparable to RSA with much smaller keys.
example: A 256-bit elliptic-curve key is commonly compared to a 3,072-bit RSA key in strength.

definition: Adi Shamir's 1979 scheme for splitting a secret into n shares so that any k shares recover it but fewer reveal nothing. It uses polynomials over a finite field.
example: A 3-of-5 scheme lets any 3 of 5 executives unlock a master key.

definition: An error-correcting code that treats data as values of a polynomial over a finite field, often GF(2⁸), so lost or corrupted symbols can be rebuilt. It is used in QR codes, CDs and storage systems.
example: A QR code can still be read with part of it covered because of Reed–Solomon correction.

definition: An integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. 1 is not prime.
example: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are prime; 9 = 3 × 3 is not.

definition: An integer greater than 1 that is not prime: it has a divisor other than 1 and itself.
example: 561 = 3 × 11 × 17 is composite.

definition: Every integer greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors.
example: 252 = 2² × 3² × 7, and no other product of primes gives 252.

definition: The number of primes up to n is approximately n / ln n, so near a large number N roughly one in ln N integers is prime.
example: Up to 1,000,000 there are 78,498 primes; 10⁶ / ln 10⁶ ≈ 72,382.

definition: Testing whether n is prime by trying to divide it by every candidate up to √n. Simple, but far too slow for numbers with hundreds of digits.
example: To test 97, try 2, 3, 5 and 7 (since √97 < 10): none divides it, so 97 is prime.

definition: An ancient algorithm that lists all primes up to N by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn. It runs in O(N log log N) time.

A fast probabilistic primality test. For a composite n, a random base wrongly passes with probability at most 1/4, so k independent rounds give at most 4⁻ᵏ. Unlike the Fermat test, it is not fooled by Carmichael numbers in general.
example: 40 rounds bound the false-pass chance for a given composite by 2⁻⁸⁰.

definition: An algorithm that makes random choices and may give a wrong answer with a small, bounded probability, in exchange for speed.
example: Miller–Rabin may wrongly accept a composite, with probability at most 1/4 per round.

definition: A widely used open-source library of cryptography and TLS code. Its RSA prime generation weeds out candidates with small factors and then runs Miller–Rabin rounds; the number of rounds depends on the version and key size.
example: openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA creates an RSA private key.

definition: Finding the prime factors of a number. No known classical algorithm does it efficiently for the product of two large random primes, which is what RSA relies on.
example: Factoring 3233 gives 61 × 53; factoring a 2,048-bit RSA modulus is believed infeasible today.

definition: Computing aᵉ mod n using the binary digits of e: square at every bit and multiply when the bit is 1, reducing mod n each time. It needs about log₂ e squarings, so a 2,048-bit exponent takes a few thousand multiplications.
example: 3¹³ mod 7 uses 13 = 1101 in binary and gives 3.

definition: Python's pow(a, e, n) computes aᵉ mod n efficiently; since Python 3.8, pow(a, -1, n) returns the modular inverse, raising ValueError if none exists.
example: pow(7, -1, 40) returns 23; pow(3, 13, 7) returns 3.

definition: Code whose running time and memory access pattern do not depend on secret values, so an attacker timing it learns nothing. Naive square-and-multiply is not constant-time because it multiplies only on 1 bits.
example: Comparing a password hash byte by byte and stopping at the first mismatch leaks timing; a constant-time comparison does not.

definition: An attack that learns secrets from how a system runs (timing, power use, cache behaviour, sound) rather than from flaws in the maths.
example: Measuring how long RSA decryption takes can leak bits of the private exponent.

definition: If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p − 1) ≡ 1 (mod p). It lets you reduce exponents mod p − 1. Its converse is false, so passing the Fermat test does not prove primality.
example: 3¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13), so 3²⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁸ ≡ 9 (mod 13).

definition: φ(n) counts the integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n. For a prime p, φ(p) = p − 1; for distinct primes p and q, φ(p × q) = (p − 1)(q − 1). φ is the Greek letter phi.
If gcd(a, n) = 1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ is Euler's totient. It generalises Fermat's little theorem and is why RSA decryption undoes encryption.
A composite n that passes the Fermat test for every base coprime to it: a^(n − 1) ≡ 1 (mod n). The smallest is 561 = 3 × 11 × 17.
example: 2⁵⁶⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 561), even though 561 is not prime.

definition: λ(n), the smallest positive m with aᵐ ≡ 1 (mod n) for every a coprime to n. For an RSA modulus n = p × q, λ(n) = lcm(p − 1, q − 1), and RSA may use it in place of φ(n).
lcm(a, b) is the smallest positive integer that both a and b divide. For positive a and b, lcm(a, b) = a × b / gcd(a, b).
The order of a modulo n is the smallest positive k with aᵏ ≡ 1 (mod n). The powers of a repeat with that period.
example: 3 has order 3 modulo 13: 3¹ = 3, 3² = 9, 3³ = 27 ≡ 1.

definition: The number n = p × q in an RSA key, the product of two secret primes. It is public; anyone who can factor it can compute the private key.
example: The toy key p = 61, q = 53 has modulus n = 3,233.

definition: The e in an RSA public key (n, e), coprime to φ(n). Encryption raises the message to the power e mod n. 65,537 (2¹⁶ + 1) is the usual choice.
example: In the toy key with n = 3,233, e = 17.

definition: The d in an RSA private key: the inverse of e modulo φ(n) (or λ(n)). Decryption raises the ciphertext to the power d mod n.
The encrypted, unreadable form of a message.
example: Toy RSA turns the message 65 into the ciphertext 2,790.

definition: The original readable message before encryption, or after decryption.
example: Decrypting the ciphertext 2,790 in toy RSA gives back the plaintext 65.

definition: RSA used directly as c = mᵉ mod n, with no padding or randomness. It is deterministic and malleable, so real systems wrap it in a padding scheme such as OAEP or PSS.
example: Encrypting "yes" twice with textbook RSA gives the same ciphertext both times, so an eavesdropper can test guesses.

definition: Encryption where the same message and key always give the same ciphertext. It leaks when two messages are equal and lets attackers test guesses.
example: Textbook RSA is deterministic; RSA-OAEP adds randomness so it is not.

definition: A cipher is malleable if an attacker can change a ciphertext into another valid ciphertext with a predictable relation to the original plaintext, without knowing it.
example: In textbook RSA, multiplying the ciphertexts of m₁ and m₂ gives a ciphertext of m₁ × m₂ (mod n).

definition: A randomised padding scheme for RSA encryption (Bellare and Rogaway, 1994), standardised in PKCS #1 (RFC 8017). It makes encryption non-deterministic and rejects tampered ciphertexts.
example: Encrypting the same message twice with RSA-OAEP gives different ciphertexts.

definition: A randomised padding scheme for RSA signatures, standardised in PKCS #1 (RFC 8017).
example: TLS 1.3 uses RSA-PSS when signing with RSA keys.

definition: A source of random-looking numbers. Ordinary RNGs (Python's random) are predictable from their output; a cryptographically secure RNG (Python's secrets, os.urandom) is designed so that its output cannot be predicted.
example: Use secrets.token_bytes(32) for a key, never random.getrandbits(256).

definition: If n₁ and n₂ are coprime, knowing x mod n₁ and x mod n₂ determines x mod n₁ × n₂ uniquely. RSA uses it to decrypt with two half-size computations mod p and mod q.
example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5) give x ≡ 8 (mod 15).

definition: A 1976 protocol by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in which two parties agree a shared secret over a public channel: each publishes gˣ mod p for a secret x, and both compute g^(xy) mod p.
example: With p = 23, g = 5, x = 6 and y = 15, both sides get the shared secret 2.

definition: Given g, p and y = gˣ mod p, find x. It is believed hard for well-chosen large groups; solving it would break Diffie–Hellman.
example: 5ˣ ≡ 8 (mod 23) has the discrete logarithm x = 6.

definition: Given g, gˣ and gʸ (mod p), compute g^(xy). Solving discrete logarithms would solve it, but it is not known to be equally hard.
example: An eavesdropper on a Diffie–Hellman exchange sees gˣ and gʸ and faces the CDH problem.

definition: Peter Shor's 1994 quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a large enough fault-tolerant quantum computer, which would break RSA and Diffie–Hellman.
example: Today's quantum hardware is far too small and noisy to factor a 2,048-bit RSA modulus.

definition: A computer that uses quantum bits and error correction robust enough to run long quantum algorithms such as Shor's. None big enough to threaten RSA exists yet.
example: A 2025 estimate by Craig Gidney puts factoring 2,048-bit RSA at about 1,400 error-corrected logical qubits, built from under a million physical qubits, running for about a week.

definition: Cryptography with a key pair: a public key anyone may use to encrypt or verify, and a private key only its owner uses to decrypt or sign. RSA and elliptic-curve schemes are examples.
example: A browser checks a server's RSA or ECDSA signature with the server's public key.

definition: A protocol by which two parties establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel, for example Diffie–Hellman.
example: A TLS handshake runs a key exchange before encrypting any page data.

definition: A fixed-size array used as a queue whose read and write positions wrap around with mod.
example: In a ring buffer of size 8, the slot after index 7 is (7 + 1) mod 8 = 0.

definition: A small value computed from data to detect accidental changes. Many checksums are sums or remainders modulo a fixed number.
example: An ISBN-10 check digit makes the weighted sum of digits divisible by 11.

definition: The Java method that returns an object's 32-bit signed int hash. It can be negative, so hashCode() % n can be negative too.
example: "polygenelubricants".hashCode() is Integer.MIN_VALUE, a negative number.

definition: The Java exception thrown when code reads or writes an array at an index below 0 or at least its length.
example: shards[-3] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -3.

definition: Daniel Shanks's algorithm for discrete logarithms that trades memory for time, taking about √N steps for a group of size N instead of N.
example: For a group of size 10¹², it needs about 10⁶ steps and stored values.

definition: An on/off switch in configuration that turns a piece of functionality on or off without redeploying code.
example: 5 independent feature flags give 2⁵ = 32 possible configurations.

definition: A value that is either true or false (1 or 0).
example: A boolean flag is_admin is either True or False.

definition: The smallest extension of a set or relation that has a required property, found by adding only what that property forces. A set is "closed under" an operation when applying the operation never leads outside it. (Not the programming sense of a function that captures variables.)
example: The transitive closure of {(1, 2), (2, 3)} adds (1, 3) and nothing else.

definition: An input that a function leaves unchanged: f(x) = x. For a permutation, it is an item that stays in its original position, so a derangement is a permutation with no fixed points. Iterative algorithms also "reach a fixed point" when another round changes nothing.
example: The permutation 1→1, 2→3, 3→2 has one fixed point, 1.

definition: The one standard representative chosen from many equivalent forms, so equal things always look the same. For an encoder, it is the one way it writes a value when several byte strings would decode to it: non-canonical inputs (extra spaces, different key order) still decode correctly but are never produced by the encoder.
example: {"a":1} and { "a": 1 } decode to the same JSON object; a canonical encoder always emits the first.

definition: Reconstructing a long DNA sequence from many short, overlapping fragments ("reads") produced by a sequencing machine. Assemblers commonly build a de Bruijn graph and look for an Euler path through it.
example: Reads ACGT, CGTA and GTAC overlap by three letters and assemble into ACGTAC.

definition: A fixed-length run of consecutive symbols that moves along a string one position at a time. A keypad that checks only the last n keys pressed is a sliding-window code tester, and a de Bruijn sequence covers every possible window.
example: In 00110 the length-2 windows are 00, 01, 11 and 10.

definition: Dividing two integers to get a whole-number quotient (and a remainder). Languages disagree on negatives: Python's // rounds down (floor), while C, C++, Java and Go truncate towards zero.
example: -7 // 3 is -3 in Python, but -7 / 3 is -2 in Java.

definition: How many times something is counted. "Counted with multiplicity" means a repeated item is counted once per occurrence, as a double root counts twice or an edge walked twice round one face counts twice.
example: (r − 2)² = 0 has the root 2 with multiplicity 2.

definition: Creating a new key pair. For RSA it means choosing two random secret primes, computing the modulus and φ(n), picking e and computing d. It needs a cryptographically secure random number generator.
example: Toy RSA key generation with p = 61 and q = 53 gives n = 3,233, e = 17 and d = 2,753.

definition: The two large secret primes p and q whose product is the RSA modulus n = p × q. Anyone who learns them can compute φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1) and then the private exponent, so they must be kept secret (or destroyed after key generation).
example: In the toy key, p = 61 and q = 53 give n = 3,233.

definition: In this app, the Data Structures & Algorithms subject, which covers graph algorithms such as BFS and Dijkstra and analysis tools such as the master theorem in depth. (In cryptography DSA can also mean the Digital Signature Algorithm, which is not meant here.)
example: The master theorem is introduced here and covered in depth in the DSA subject.

definition: Giving radio transmitters frequencies so that transmitters close enough to interfere get different ones. Modelled as graph colouring: transmitters are vertices, interfering pairs are edges and frequencies are colours.
example: Three mutually interfering mobile masts form a triangle and need 3 different frequencies.

definition: A polygon with no dents: every interior angle is less than 180°, so the straight line between any two points inside it stays inside it. Its diagonals never leave the shape, which is why triangulations of convex polygons are easy to count.
example: A regular hexagon is convex; a star shape is not.

definition: John Hopcroft and Robert Tarjan's 1974 algorithm that decides whether a graph is planar in linear time, O(n) for n vertices, using depth-first search. (Not Hopcroft's DFA-minimisation algorithm.)
example: It can check a road map with a million junctions for planarity with work proportional to its size.
